grammar.title: Identifying people and things
grammar.summary: Each personal pronoun is made plural by adding the suffix 哋 dei6.
grammar.body: Each of the personal pronoun can be made plural by the addition of 哋 dei6

grammar.title: The suffix dei6
grammar.summary: dei6 only pluralises pronouns; its other uses are the indefinite pronoun jan4 dei6 and contracted forms with names.
grammar.body:
The suffix dei6 cannot be used to form plural forms of nouns (e.g., we cannot use 先生哋 sin1 saang1 dei6 to mean “teachers”)
Apart from the personal pronouns as shown above its only uses are:
In the form 人哋 jan4 dei6 which serves as a kind of indefinite pronoun (people, one, etc.)
This form can also be used to refer indirectly to oneself
In contracted forms with names, as in: Paul keoi5 dei6 —> Paul dei6; aa3 Can2 keoi5 dei6 —> aa3 Can2 dei6

examples.jp: A: nei5 dim2 gaai2 m4 ceot1 seng1 gaa3?
B: jan4 dei6 m4 hou2 ji3 si1 aa3
aa3 Can2 keoi5 dei6 —> aa3 Can2 dei6

grammar.title: Using pronouns
grammar.summary: Pronouns introduce and identify people, but both subject and object pronouns are dropped when understood from context; in a self-introduction ngo5 is used only once.
grammar.body:
Pronouns are used to refer to individuals, as in introductions
Pronouns can be omitted when they are understood from the context
Pro-drop also applies to objects
When several statement are made about the same subjects, it is usually understood after its first mention, in self-introduction, it is sufficient to use ngo5 once

examples.jp: A: aa3 Jing1 zou6 mat1 je5 gung1 gaa3?
examples.en: What does Ying do for a living?

examples.jp: A: jam2 m4 jam2 zau2 aa3?
B: m4 jam2 laa3, m4 goi1
A: ni1 go3 sung3 bei2 nei5 ge3
B: do1 ze6! ngo5 hou2 zung1 ji3 aa3!
examples.lit: Thank you! I very much like!

examples.jp: ngo5 giu3 Mary, gam1 nin2 sap6 baat3 seoi3, lai4 hoeng1 gong2 zou6 gaau1 wun6 hok6 saang1
examples.en: My name is Mary. [I'm] 18 this year, [I] came to Hong Kong as an exchange student
examples.lit: I called Mary, this year 18 years old, come Hong Kong as exchange student

grammar.title: The third person: keoi5 he, she and it
grammar.summary: keoi5 has no gender and normally does not translate English 'it'; things are simply left unmentioned.
grammar.body:
It does not differentiate gender, normally do not correspond to the English pronoun it.
For example when referring to a picture or a piece of clothing
A sequence of statement can be made about the same topic

examples.jp: hou2 leng3 aa3! ngo5 jiu3 aa3!
keoi5 maai5 zo2 gaa3 san1 ce1 hou2 gwai3 ge3, hou2 coi2 keoi5 taai3 taai2 dou1 hou2 zung1 ji3 ze1
examples.en: He's bought a new car, [it was] very expensive, fortunately his wife likes [it] too
examples.lit: He bought a new car, very expensive, fortunately his wife also likes

grammar.title: No counterpart to “it”
grammar.summary: Cantonese has no dummy subject 'it' for weather or general statements.
grammar.body: Whether it is referring to the weather, or to nothing in particular

grammar.title: Reflexive zi6 gei2
grammar.summary: 自己 zi6 gei2 is the reflexive for all persons: used alone, to reinforce a pronoun, or as an adverb 'by oneself'.
grammar.body:
The reflexive form 自己 zi6 gei2 is used for all persons: myself, yourself, herself, ourselves, etc. It is used:
(i) Alone, referring back to the subject of the sentence
(ii) Reinforcing a pronoun
(iii) As an adverb meaning “by oneself”

examples.jp: nei5 jiu3 siu2 sam1 ziu3 gu3 zi6 gei2
examples.en: You should look after yourself carefully
examples.lit: You should carefully look after yourself

examples.en: Don't blame yourself all the time

examples.lit: I myself not would so do

examples.lit: I myself buy groceries cook rice

examples.jp: keoi5 soeng2 zi6 gei2 zou6 hai6 zyu2 jam6
examples.en: He wants to be the department chairperson himself
examples.lit: He want self do department chairperson

grammar.title: Addressing people
grammar.summary: Surnames come before titles (and before personal names) in Cantonese.
grammar.body:
Unlike English, Chinese surnames are always given before titles
As well as other titles like president, doctor, professor, ambassador, sister
Personal name follow the surname, Mr. John Smith —> Smith John Mr. in Cantonese
This shows the great stress in which Chinese people have traditionally placed on the family

grammar.title: Adjectives or verbs? Both!
grammar.summary: All adjectives can also act as descriptive verbs: hou2 means both 'good' and 'to be good'.
grammar.body:
Hou2 means good, nice, well, fine, OK, and so on.
As in English, adjectives go in front of nouns
In Cantonese, all adjectives can also act as verbs to describe things (descriptive verbs) and so hou2 means not only good also to be good
All adjectives behave the same. ugly (cau2) also means to be ugly

grammar.title: Simple questions
grammar.summary: Adding maa3? to the end of a sentence makes a question, but in Cantonese this is used only for polite questions.
grammar.body:
In Mandarin (now usually known as Putonghua, the official common language of China) you can ask a question simply by putting the word ma? on the end of the sentence
You can also do the same in Cantonese, but less common.
The only time is when you are asking a polite question

grammar.title: Two for the price of one + Follow-up question
grammar.summary: hou2 also means 'very' (hou2 hou2 = very good); the particle ne1? asks a follow-up question without repeating what went before.
grammar.body:
When you learned hou2 you got double value, because it not only means good, well, but very as well.
So means A special kind of shortcut question is formed with the little ne1? This asks a follow-up question without the tedium of repeating in full what went before

grammar.title: dou1 also
grammar.summary: dou1 'also, too' always comes just before the verb; verbs have only one form regardless of tense or subject.
grammar.body:
dou1 means also, too. It always comes just before a verb
Verbs only have one form! The same word hou2 was translated as am well, is well, and are well in our earlier examples. Regardless of the tense, the mood, the subject or anything else, the verb will always be simply hou2. This applies to all verbs, there are no irregularities.

grammar.title: People (jan4)
grammar.summary: jan4 means both 'person' and 'people'; nouns have no plural form, so number is read from context.
grammar.body: Jan4 means person but it also means people. In fact, all nouns in Cantonese are the same whether single or plural and you can only tell which is meant from the sense of the conversation. These is usually no problem by looking the personal pronouns you can easily tell which is which

examples.jp: keoi5 dei6 hai6 jat1 baan1 jan4
examples.en: They are a group of people

grammar.title: hai6 to be
grammar.summary: 係 hai6 introduces noun phrases (and can often be omitted); it is not used with adjectives. hai6 aa3 / m4 hai6 aa3 answer questions, but hai6 agrees with the statement rather than meaning 'yes', and most questions are answered by repeating the verb.
grammar.body:
Hai6 ‘to be’ is used to introduce noun phrases, as in making introductions and identifying people
But many such statements can also be made without hai6
Hai6 is not used with predicative adjectives, which are typically introduced by hou2 (lit. very): ngo5 ji4 gaa1 hou2 mong4 (Not *ngo5 ji4 gaa1 hai6 hou2 mong4); nei5 gaa1 ze1 hou2 leng3 (Not *nei5 gaa1 ze1 hai6 hou2 leng3); ngo5 tung4 keoi5 hou2 suk6 (Not *ngo5 tung4 keoi5 hai6 hou2 suk6)
Hai6 also serves to indicate agreement and as an answer to certain types of question, Hai6 meaning ‘yes’ and its negative form m4 hai6 ‘no’
hai6 shouldn't be taken simply as a counterpart to English ‘yes’ since (i) hai6 can indicate agreement with a negative sentence
The most common type of question do not take hai6 for an answer, instead the verb of the original question is repeated

examples.jp: ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 naam4 pang4 jau5
ni1 go3 ngo5 naam4 pang4 jau5
examples.en: This is my boyfriend (alternative without hai6)

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 hai6 ciu4 zau1 jan4

examples.en: We are Chiu Chow (people) (alternative without hai6)

examples.jp: A: nei5 zan1 hai6 seon3 me1?
A: keoi5 dei6 mei6 dou3 me1?
A: ngo5 dei6 heoi3 m4 heoi3 maai5 je5 aa3?

grammar.title: Negatives m4
grammar.summary: 唔 m4 'not' always comes in front of the word it negates.
grammar.body: The word for not is m4. It always comes in front of the word it refers to

examples.jp: Wong4 sin1 saang1 m4 leng3 zai2

grammar.title: Another way to ask questions
grammar.summary: The commonest question form pairs the positive and negative of the verb (leng3 m4 leng3) and adds the particle aa3?; the answer repeats the verb.
grammar.body:
The most common way to ask a question in Cantonese is by using the positive and negative of a verb together and adding the little word “aa3?” at the end of the sentence
What you are really doing is offering your listener a choice of answers (She pretty? Not pretty? Eh?) and the answer is going to be either keoi5 leng3 or keoi5 m4 leng3
In the same way to you can ask: nei5 maai6 m4 maai6 ce1 aa3?
Cantonese people like to have a comfortable noise to round off their sentences with and they have a whole string of little words (usually called particles) which they use. Aa3? Has no meaning on its own, it is just used to punch home the question which has been asked in the sentence. Maa3? And ne1? Which we have already met are other examples of particles.

examples.jp: nei5 maai6 m4 maai6 ce1 aa3?

grammar.title: The unspoken if
grammar.summary: Cantonese often omits any word for 'if', letting the conditional meaning flow from context.
grammar.body:
There are various words for if in Cantonese, but quite often none of them is used, the meaning seeming to flow naturally from the context.
In the dialogue the sentence: nei5 m4 jiu3, Lei5 siu2 ze2 jiu3 m4 jiu3 aa3?

examples.jp: nei5 m4 jiu3, Lei5 siu2 ze2 jiu3 m4 jiu3 aa3?
examples.en: If you don't want one, does Miss Li?
examples.lit: You not want, Miss Li want not want, eh?

notes.title: Cantonese surnames
notes.body: The most common: Wong 王，黄 wong4; Cheung 张 zoeng1; Ho 何 ho4; Lee 李 lei5; Leung 梁 loeng4; Chan 陈 can4

notes.title: Names and family
notes.body: Surnames are always given before titles (Wong4 sin1 saang1 = Mr. Wong) and before personal names (Mr. John Smith —> Smith John Mr.). This shows the great stress in which Chinese people have traditionally placed on the family.
